## Code navigation

- Start any task by asking a relevant high level question with `slopdex faq "<frequently asked question>"`
- To discover relevant file run `slopdex map -g "<glob>" -i -e "<term|term>" -q "<short symbol concept>" -q "<additional concept>" --private --callers 2 --callees 2 <paths...>` and immediately read plausible implementation ranges from the source files directly.
- Avoid mapping repeatedly, frontload the map in one call.
- Slopdex is not a replacement for other search tools, but an addition that provides semantic symbol search and mapping functionality.
- To rename or move symbols/functions or files, use `slopdex refactor <src> <dest>` with src an dest being a file and an optional symbol like `src/parser.ts::parse`. This correctly updates references for supported languages.

tasks.prompt: Investigate this Excalidraw checkout. A user selects an arrow that carries a caption, presses on the caption with the selection tool and slides the pointer: the caption follows, but stays glued to the arrow's route (straight, bent or orthogonal), and the arrow remembers where along its route the caption sits so later reshaping keeps it there. Identify exactly 6 implementation functions by these semantic roles: (1) the selection-tool pointer-move hook that claims the gesture whenever it began on the caption, switches the cursor to a closed hand, and only starts moving anything once the pointer has travelled past a zoom-scaled distance or a move is already underway; (2) the editor-level step that turns the pointer, minus the grab offset recorded at press time, into a fraction along the route, writes that fraction plus re-centred coordinates onto the caption, and flags the editor as mid-gesture; (3) the routine returning the 0..1 share of total arc length nearest a scene location, choosing the nearest piece of the route and converting its local t value into accumulated length, or nothing for an empty or zero-length route; (4) the per-arrow memo that splits the route into pieces, measures each, builds running totals, and is invalidated by the shape's revision counter; (5) the decomposition that turns an arrow into ordered pieces, treating orthogonal arrows as sharp-cornered straight runs and otherwise returning either the bent pieces or the straight ones, never a mix; (6) the math-package search for the Bezier t value nearest a location: coarse sampling at evenly spaced values, then a shrinking-window refinement around the best sample. Explain how one pointer move flows through these, then answer: What keeps the caption from jumping so its centre sits under the cursor when grabbed? If the press lands where the caption overlaps the middle-segment knob, which wins? Is a sub-threshold move still claimed by the hook? For an orthogonal arrow with rounded corners, does the caption follow the rounded corners? Base your explanation on this checkout's implementation; do not modify code.
tasks.title: Sliding an arrow caption along its route

tasks.prompt: Investigate this Excalidraw checkout. A user selects an ellipse holding a caption that contains a very long unbroken token (such as a URL) and some trailing spaces, then presses Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+> several times. Each press scales the type by about ten percent; the caption reflows inside the oval, the oval grows as needed, and the caption is re-centred. Identify exactly 6 implementation functions by these semantic roles: (1) the shared routine behind the bigger/smaller-type commands and the explicit picker that rewrites every selected piece of writing via a caller-supplied rule, re-lays each one out, keeps free-standing auto-width writing visually anchored per its alignment, afterwards refreshes connectors attached to the writing, and only remembers a new default when all results agree; (2) the relayout step that re-breaks the original unbroken source to the host's usable width, re-measures it, enlarges the host's height and/or width when the measurement no longer fits, and repositions the writing inside the host; (3) the inverse sizing formula giving the outer host extent required for an inner measurement, with different padding multipliers for ovals, rhombi, connectors and everything else; (4) the source-of-truth row breaker that returns visual rows with source offsets, falls back to hard breaks only when the available width is non-finite or negative, and keeps any already-fitting hard row untouched; (5) the fallback that splits a single over-long token glyph by glyph using cached per-glyph advances, leaving multi-codepoint emoji intact; (6) the finishing step for the final visual row of a hard row, which strips trailing whitespace only when the row overflows and then re-admits as many whitespace characters as still fit. Explain how one key press flows through these, then answer: When does the oval widen rather than only grow taller? Why is the alignment-anchoring step a no-op for the caption inside the oval? How are trailing spaces treated at an internal soft break versus at the end of a hard row? What is stored as the remembered default when several selected captions end with different values? Base your explanation on this checkout's implementation; do not modify code.
tasks.title: Stepping up caption type inside an oval

tasks.prompt: Investigate this Excalidraw checkout. A user selects a captioned rectangle, an ellipse, an orthogonal connector between them, and a straight connector from the rectangle to an unselected diamond, then moves the turn knob while holding Shift. Everything swings around the selection's centre in set increments, the orthogonal connector is re-routed, and the straight connector lets go of the diamond. Identify exactly 6 implementation functions by these semantic roles: (1) the selection-tool pointer-move gatekeeper for transform knobs that defers to the cropping editor, refuses to turn selections containing frames or to transform a lone orthogonal connector, waits for a deliberate move when Alt is held on a scaling knob, snaps the pointer, and decides when proportional scaling is the default; (2) the group-turning routine that derives one shared angle from the pointer around the pivot, moves each member's centre around that pivot by the incremental amount while setting its absolute angle to original plus shared, and re-derives orthogonal connectors from their attachments instead of turning them; (3) the helper converting an orthogonal connector's two attachment locations into the connector's own relative coordinates so it can be re-routed; (4) the conversion from a stored proportional attachment ratio into a scene location on the target shape, honouring the shape's own angle; (5) the routine detaching one end of a connector, which removes the connector from the target's back-reference list only if the opposite end is not attached to the same target, and returns the former target's id; (6) the placement routine for a caption inside a host, honouring vertical and horizontal alignment, special-casing a sticky note's footer, and swinging the caption's centre around the host's content centre when the host is angled. Explain how one pointer move flows through these, then answer: Is the Shift increment applied by rounding or by flooring? What happens to the straight connector's two ends and to the diamond's back-references? Does the orthogonal connector's own angle change, and what is passed to it? What happens if a frame is part of the selection? Base your explanation on this checkout's implementation; do not modify code.
tasks.title: Turning a multi-selection with attached connectors

tasks.prompt: Investigate this Excalidraw checkout. A user clicks where a turned, rounded-corner, unfilled rectangle lies over a filled ellipse; depending on whether the click lands on the stroke, near a rounded corner, or in the empty interior, the rectangle or the ellipse is picked. Identify exactly 8 implementation functions by these semantic roles: (1) the editor method that, given every candidate under the pointer ordered back to front, may prefer a selected one, else re-checks the front-most with half the usual tolerance and otherwise falls back to the one directly beneath; (2) the per-candidate editor predicate that short-circuits on a selected item's transform box, then accepts contact with the item's caption, before delegating to precise geometry; (3) the tolerance rule: the larger of half the stroke width plus a hair and a zoom-scaled base reach times a fudge factor; (4) the precise geometric check with a single-entry memo whose reuse depends on whether the remembered answer was positive or negative relative to the new tolerance, a cheap turned-box rejection, and a choice between interior-plus-outline and outline-only; (5) the policy deciding whether an interior counts: never for arrows, only closed loops for lines and freehand strokes, else when non-transparently filled, captioned, embedded content, writing or a picture; (6) the containment check casting a segment from the location away from the box centre and using the parity of distinct outline crossings, with a fill-polygon path for closed freehand strokes; (7) the how-far-from-the-outline calculation for box-like shapes that un-turns the location around the centre and takes the minimum over edges and corner arcs; (8) the cached decomposition of a box-like shape into four inset edges and four cubic corner arcs, substituting a tiny radius for sharp corners. Explain the flow, then answer: Which shape is picked for a click in the rectangle's empty interior, and why? If the rectangle is already selected, what does (1) return for that click, and which option changes it? Why are crossings de-duplicated? How does the memo avoid returning a stale miss when tolerance grows? Base your explanation on this checkout's implementation; do not modify code.
tasks.title: Deciding which overlapping shape a click picks

tasks.prompt: Investigate this Excalidraw checkout. A user moves the end knob of an existing straight arrow over a large unfilled rectangle that encloses a smaller filled card drawn above it; a highlight suggests the target. The default, non-experimental policy applies. Identify exactly 8 implementation functions by these semantic roles: (1) the editor step moving selected vertices: collapses interior picks on orthogonal arrows to the last vertex, computes the delta with Shift angle-locking or grid snapping, applies the changes, lifts the arrow above its target, and records a one-time alternative focus for the other end; (2) the module-private computation that asks the policy about both ends, turns the answers into records or detachments plus a highlight, then simulates the moved arrow to re-seat attached ends; (3) the default per-end policy choosing keep, detach, attach-on-outline or attach-inside: detaching when both ends move or attaching is toggled off, delegating orthogonal arrows, handling both ends on one shape, and forcing inside with Alt; (4) the selector picking one target by smallest absolute outline gap, yielding to a smaller overlapping shape that contains the location when overlap and area ratios are met; (5) the front-to-back scan gathering attachable shapes within reach that honours frame clipping, lets locked shapes occlude without being gathered, and stops at the first opaque shape containing the location; (6) the signed proximity measure: -Infinity when bounds miss or the location is within a frame, positive gap inside, negated gap outside only within tolerance; (7) the outline-aiming helper that tries an edge-midpoint snap, else casts a ray from the neighbouring vertex (or the other end's stored attachment) through the location against the shape's two corner-to-corner axes, keeping the nearer crossing if inside; (8) the conversion of a scene location into the proportional ratio stored on the attachment record, un-turning around the centre, centring degenerate shapes and flooring the divisor. Explain the flow, then answer: Why is the large rectangle never gathered while the knob is over the card? What mode and focus result just outside the card's outline? What does Alt change? Base your explanation on this checkout's implementation; do not modify code.
tasks.title: Attaching a moved arrow end among nested shapes

tasks.prompt: Investigate this Excalidraw checkout. With the eraser tool, a user sweeps the pointer across the canvas: shapes the stroke touches fade as it passes, holding Alt while sweeping back un-fades them, and on release the faded shapes disappear in one undoable step; a plain click without moving removes whatever sits under the cursor. Identify exactly 6 implementation functions by these semantic roles: (1) the editor-level hook invoked on every drag-phase move while this tool is active, which feeds the newest scene coordinate to the stroke-tracking object, passes the Alt state as a give-back flag, and replaces the pending set before repainting; (2) that object's private routine that takes only the newest stroke segment, tests every unlocked visible shape against it, and grows or shrinks the pending set, pulling in all members of the outermost enclosing cluster plus a shape's label or a label's host; (3) the per-shape contact predicate that starts with an inflated box overlap, treats interiors as hits for some shapes, uses a zoom-dependent tolerance for pen strokes, and segment distance for open polylines; (4) the shared shape-kind rule deciding whether a shape's interior counts as touchable (filled, labeled, embedded or textual; closed loops only for pen strokes and lines; never arrows); (5) the point query returning every hit shape under a coordinate, ignoring locked shapes and hosted labels, discarding hits clipped away by an enclosing artboard, and moving embedded web content to the end; (6) the release-time commit that detaches arrow attachments without recording separate history, flags pending shapes plus artboard contents and hosted labels as gone, and requests a single capture. Trace how pointer movement and release reach these functions, then answer: How does the stroke decide between adding and removing candidates, and why is the cluster bookkeeping needed when giving shapes back? For freehand strokes, what tolerance and fallback containment test apply? What exactly does a zero-distance click remove, and how is the distance measured? Why are attachments patched with a raw mutation rather than through the normal history path? Base your explanation on this checkout's implementation; do not modify code.
tasks.title: Eraser sweep marking, restoring and committing removals

tasks.prompt: Investigate this Excalidraw checkout. A user draws a freeform loop around shapes to pick them, either with the dedicated loop tool or by holding Alt in the middle of a rectangle drag. Depending on the box-selection preference, shapes must either be fully encircled or merely crossed; grouped shapes, artboards and Shift-additive picking all behave specially. Identify exactly 6 implementation functions by these semantic roles: (1) the editor's drag-phase move handler (installed at press time, not the hover handler) that converts an in-progress rectangle marquee into a freeform loop starting at the press origin when Alt is held, and falls back to the rectangle when Alt is released; (2) the loop object's private per-move routine that rebuilds the stored outline segments of visible shapes only when scroll or zoom changed, then computes the picked set with a zoom-scaled path simplification; (3) the pure geometric resolver that, per shape, clips to the part visible inside its artboard, prefilters by boxes, and classifies shapes as enclosed or crossed according to the mode; (4) the helper used only in the fully-encircled mode that drops members of an outermost cluster unless every eligible member was picked; (5) the loop object's state-commit step that merges the previous pick for additive gestures, strips contents of picked artboards, widens to clusters, and opens a line editor when exactly one polyline remains; (6) the memoised inner worker (not the exported wrapper that resolves the picked shapes and handles the empty case) that widens a picked set to whole clusters while respecting the cluster currently being edited and demoting single-member clusters. Explain the flow from pointer move to editor state, then answer: When a loop partially circles a two-member cluster, what ends up picked in each mode, and which function makes the difference? Why are the stored outlines invalidated on viewport change, and what tolerance is used to simplify the path? How are locked shapes and hosted labels treated? What happens to a picked artboard's contents? Base your explanation on this checkout's implementation; do not modify code.
tasks.title: Freeform loop selection with clusters and artboards

tasks.prompt: Investigate this Excalidraw checkout. A user starts dragging some shapes and presses Alt mid-drag: the originals snap back to where the drag began while identical copies keep following the pointer, carrying their labels, arrow attachments, cluster memberships and artboard (frame) relationships. Identify exactly 8 implementation functions by these semantic roles: (1) the editor helper, invoked at most once per drag, that clones the moving set, resets the originals to their press-time positions, swaps the press bookkeeping (hit target, hit list, drag origin) over to the copies, and replaces the scene synchronously; (2) the per-object cloning step that gives a copy a fresh identity and timestamps, optionally a new roughness seed, and remaps cluster ids through a shared old-to-new table; (3) the recursive structural cloner that handles plain objects and arrays but skips the top-level memoised drawing artefacts; (4) the tiny revision helper that increments the counter, rolls a new random tiebreaker and stamps the time without notifying anyone; (5) the reordering pass, run before cloning, that makes the members of every cluster contiguous level by level from the outermost cluster inward, keeping first-appearance order and bailing out if anything would be lost; (6) the post-cloning fixer in the attachment module that rewrites label, host and arrow-endpoint references to point at copies, drops references whose target was not cloned, and re-routes right-angle connectors; (7) the fixer that points each copy's artboard membership at the clone of its original's artboard, or at none; (8) the editor method that, only when snapping applies, recomputes the stored spacing between neighbouring shapes used for equal-distance guides. Trace the call path from the drag handler through these, then answer: After cloning, which set sits higher in stacking order, and which set continues to move? Right after cloning, which artboard does a copy of an artboard child belong to when the artboard itself was not cloned, and why? What happens to an arrow cloned without the shape it was attached to? Is the roughness seed randomised once or twice for these copies? Base your explanation on this checkout's implementation; do not modify code.
tasks.title: Alt-drag cloning of a moving selection

tasks.prompt: Investigate this Excalidraw checkout. A user presses undo after removing a shape that had arrows attached and an empty label. The editor restores it, repairs attachments both ways, fixes stacking, skips entries that change nothing on screen, and announces the result without re-recording it. Ignore the keyboard dispatch and the stack-walking loop; identify exactly 8 implementation functions by these semantic roles: (1) the history-entry-level step that enacts the element part of the entry with revision counters excluded, falling back on the store's snapshot for elements missing from the scene, then enacts the editor-state part and ORs the two on-screen-change answers (not the static store-level variant that uses an empty snapshot); (2) the factory producing the per-bucket enactor, which also infers whether the replay runs forward or backward from revision numbers; (3) the method that, after patches land, unhooks dangling references to removed objects and re-establishes two-way links for added or link-touching updates, adjusting revision counters by direction and folding the resulting edits back into the entry; (4) the comparator that reduces before and after states to what actually paints, treating missing, deleted or empty unattached labels as nothing, and ignores metadata fields and references to empty labels; (5) the sorter used to restore stacking, breaking ties by id and keeping array position when a position key is absent; (6) the element-level method that rewrites the entry with current scene values for every key except the attachment list, dropping per-object patches that no longer differ; (7) the snapshot method that returns the same instance when nothing changed and only compares hashes in the deferred capture mode; (8) the store's publishing step for undoable updates that reuses an already computed delta instance rather than recomputing. Trace the path, then answer: How is the replay direction decided, and how does it affect revision numbers of repaired neighbours? Why can one undo press skip several entries after an empty label was removed? When is re-sorting skipped entirely? Why isn't the published update pushed onto the undo stack again? Base your explanation on this checkout's implementation; do not modify code.
tasks.title: Enacting an undo entry: repair, stacking and visibility

tasks.prompt: Investigate this Excalidraw checkout. A user picks several shapes, some inside an artboard and some outside, possibly while drilled into an existing cluster, and presses Ctrl+G. The command must decide whether it is available at all, nest the new cluster correctly, detach members from their artboards when they come from different ones, keep the members adjacent in stacking order, pick the new cluster, and become a single undo step. Identify exactly 8 implementation functions by these semantic roles (the command object's own body is not one of them): (1) the availability gate shared by the command and its toolbar button, requiring two or more picked shapes while ignoring hosted labels; (2) the check, honouring the cluster currently being edited, of whether every picked shape already shares some cluster; (3) the predicate rejecting a multi-shape pick that contains both an artboard and one of its own contents; (4) the filter keeping artboards plus shapes whose artboard isn't part of the same set; (5) the routine that clears artboard membership for the given shapes and their hosted labels via in-place mutation; (6) the pure list helper deciding where the new cluster id is spliced into a shape's ordered membership list; (7) the helper producing the next picked-state for one cluster id, refusing to mark clusters with fewer than two members; (8) the store's precedence rule choosing which single capture mode wins when several were requested before one commit. Trace the flow from the keystroke through the command result being applied and committed, then answer: When is the command a silent no-op versus unavailable? While editing a nested cluster, where does the new id land relative to the edited cluster's id, and what does that mean for nesting? Where in stacking order do the members end up, and does their internal order change? If something else in the same tick asks for a never-undoable update, which capture mode wins? Base your explanation on this checkout's implementation; do not modify code.
tasks.title: Ctrl+G clustering across artboards and nested edits

tasks.prompt: Investigate this Excalidraw checkout. A user selects exactly one frame, opens the picture-saving dialog with 'only selected', dark output and 'embed scene' switched on, and saves a PNG; later they keep using that saved file as their working document. Identify exactly 8 implementation functions by these semantic roles: (1) the editor-instance handler the dialog calls, which runs the save, silences a cancelled save picker, shows other failures as an on-screen error, and only under specific conditions adopts the returned handle as the working document; (2) the routine deciding which part of the drawing is handed over, based on the 'only selected' toggle, treating a lone selected artboard specially and deep-copying the result; (3) the filter keeping shapes whose bounding boxes intersect an artboard while excluding shapes owned by a different artboard; (4) the dispatcher that turns editor settings into output options and routes to vector file, vector-to-system-clipboard, raster file or raster-to-clipboard; (5) the async step that re-sanitizes the shapes, picks theme and background colours, waits for typefaces and computes output size, scale and origin offset; (6) the tiny helper translating artboard decoration options into outline/title/clipping flags, overriding them when a single artboard is the subject; (7) the function that allocates the bitmap, decodes pictures used by picture shapes, and paints everything into it; (8) the helper that splices the serialized drawing into the raster file's chunk list. Explain the call flow from the dialog button to the bytes written. Also answer: when one artboard is the subject, which decorations end up drawn, how is clipping actually achieved, and what happens to padding? Where in the chunk sequence does the drawing go, and is it compressed? How are the bitmap's pixel sizes rounded, and what background is still used when the background toggle is off? Exactly when does the editor start treating the saved PNG as the working document? Base your explanation on this checkout's implementation; do not modify code.
tasks.title: Saving one frame as a PNG that carries the editable drawing

tasks.prompt: Investigate this Excalidraw checkout. A user saves a drawing as an .excalidraw.svg with the drawing embedded; it contains two picture shapes sharing one uploaded photo (one of them cropped) plus a removed shape that referenced another photo. Later they drop the file back onto the editor. Identify exactly 6 implementation functions by these semantic roles: (1) the vector document builder that creates the root node with its metadata and definitions children, optionally embeds the drawing while swallowing any failure, registers one clip region per artboard, inlines typefaces, paints a backdrop rectangle and finally emits shapes; (2) the helper that writes marker comments plus a text blob into the metadata node; (3) the text packer producing a versioned byte-string record, deflating unless told not to and silently falling back to an uncompressed record if deflating throws; (4) the serializer-side pruner that keeps only stored binary assets still referenced by live shapes; (5) the per-shape vector emitter that, for picture shapes, defines each asset once as a reusable symbol and references it from each occurrence; (6) the reader that finds the embedded block in raw markup, tells payload generations apart, accepts an old unwrapped JSON form, and maps problems onto two distinct error kinds. Explain how the drawing travels from the save action into the markup and back into JSON text. Also answer: is the embedded drawing compressed here, and why is the blob converted to base64 without a second UTF-8 pass? Does a failure while embedding abort the save? How many symbols are created for the two picture shapes, what makes the cropped one distinct, and what changes when symbol reuse is disabled? What separates the 'no embedded drawing' outcome from the 'corrupt drawing' outcome, and how is the oldest generation's text decoded? Base your explanation on this checkout's implementation; do not modify code.
tasks.title: Vector output that embeds the editable drawing and reads it back

tasks.prompt: Investigate this Excalidraw checkout. A user clicks the toolbar's picture button and chooses four photos at once: a WebP saved with a .png extension, a 9000-pixel JPEG, a small vector logo, and a truncated file that the browser cannot decode. Identify exactly 8 implementation functions by these semantic roles: (1) the editor method that creates stand-in shapes for the whole batch, lays them out, initializes each in parallel, turns failures into removed shapes with an error message, re-lays out the survivors and selects them in one undoable update; (2) the layout routine arranging units in a roughly square arrangement of rows centred on a point; (3) the upload fixer that re-labels an incoming blob's declared type from its suffix or its contents, and marks it so the work is never repeated; (4) the magic-number sniffer inspecting the leading bytes; (5) the per-upload initializer that sanitizes vector markup, derives a content-hash identity, applies size limits only to assets not stored yet, registers the asset and waits for decoding before sizing the shape; (6) the downscaler that leaves vector graphics alone, short-circuits when already small enough, and otherwise lazily pulls in a resampling library; (7) the package-level routine that turns stored data URLs into decoded bitmaps, publishing the in-flight promise before awaiting it and reporting which assets failed (not the editor wrapper that flags shapes as broken); (8) the sizing helper fitting the decoded bitmap's intrinsic pixel size under a viewport-relative height cap and recentring it on the stand-in. Explain the flow from the click to the final selected shapes. Also answer: why is the identity derived before shrinking, and is a failed shrink fatal? When is the byte limit enforced? What happens to the stand-in of the undecodable file? Why is the latest version of the stand-in re-read, and when are the intrinsic sizes not applied? Does content sniffing run for a file named *.excalidraw? Base your explanation on this checkout's implementation; do not modify code.
tasks.title: Adding several photos: type sniffing, shrinking, hashing and decoding

tasks.prompt: Investigate this Excalidraw checkout. The editor component mounts with initial data containing labels in two hand-drawn typefaces and a code typeface; the first paint uses fallback glyphs, then the real glyphs arrive and text must be re-laid out. Identify exactly 6 implementation functions by these semantic roles: (1) the editor component's own startup routine (not the hosting web app's) that sanitizes the initial data, resets undo state, applies it, and then kicks off typeface fetching using the restored default typeface rather than live state; (2) the per-instance warm-up that collects the typefaces in use and adds the default one with a fixed sample string; (3) the collector mapping each typeface index to the set of glyph characters used, reading the unwrapped source text rather than the displayed text; (4) the static routine that adds every non-system face to the document's face set and then drives at most ten concurrent fetches, flattening and filtering the results; (5) the generic bounded-concurrency helper method that gathers fulfilled results keyed by their original order index; (6) the callback that dedups by a style/weight/range signature, then discards cached drawings of text and their containers plus glyph-width measurements, and requests a repaint. Explain the flow from mount to the repaint. Also answer: which sample characters are used for the default typeface and when? Which registered faces are never added to the face set? When is a typeface skipped without any fetch, and what happens when one fetch fails? When does the callback bail out early, and what is still recorded even then? Besides startup, which other events invoke that callback? Base your explanation on this checkout's implementation; do not modify code.
tasks.title: Warming typefaces at startup and repainting text once they arrive

tasks.prompt: Investigate this Excalidraw checkout. A user opens a years-old drawing file. It has a label storing size and typeface as one combined string like "20px Virgil" with no spacing ratio, a polyline of the retired freehand-era type whose first vertex is not at the origin, an arrow with a single valid vertex, and a label that references a host shape whose attachment list does not mention it. Identify exactly 6 implementation functions by these semantic roles: (1) the lookup turning a legacy typeface word into its numeric identifier, with a default for unknown words; (2) the step choosing a vertical spacing ratio for an old label, preferring an inferred value and falling back to the per-typeface constant; (3) the measurement helper inferring that ratio from the stored box height, the number of text rows and the size; (4) the vertex sanitizer that drops malformed vertices and synthesizes a two-vertex segment from stored width and height when too few survive; (5) the low-level module-private helper that subtracts the first vertex from every vertex and reports the shift (not the public wrapper that also moves the shape's origin); (6) the integrity fixer for a label attached to a host: clears the reference when the host is gone, copies the host's rotation except for connectors, and appends itself to the host's attachment list when missing. Explain the call flow from opening the file to these helpers. Also answer: when is the spacing-ratio step skipped entirely, and when is the inferred value rejected? Which shape type does the retired polyline become, and under what condition is it re-anchored? What does the single-vertex arrow end up with? Under which option does the attachment fixer run at all, and what does it do for a removed label whose host exists? Base your explanation on this checkout's implementation; do not modify code.
tasks.title: Migrating ancient labels and polylines on file open

tasks.prompt: Investigate this Excalidraw checkout. In a live shared room, Alice drops a photo onto the canvas. Bob first sees an empty placeholder, then the picture appears. The shape travels over the realtime channel; the bytes go through cloud object storage. Identify exactly 8 implementation functions by these semantic roles: (1) the generic tracker method, shared by every storage backend, that walks the canvas, selects picture payloads whose revision is neither already persisted nor currently in flight, hands them to an injected backend callback, and records per-item outcomes (not the room-specific callback that is injected into it); (2) the app helper that turns each picture's data URI into an encrypted envelope with mime type and timestamps, refusing oversized pictures; (3) the shared editor-package routine that lays out that binary envelope as a JSON header, an IV, and an encrypted, deflated inner bundle of metadata plus payload; (4) the cloud bucket writer that pushes all envelopes in parallel with cache headers and reports which ids succeeded or failed; (5) the predicate deciding which picture shapes that are still marked as awaiting may now be flipped to ready, which is what tells peers to go and get the bytes; (6) on Bob's side, the room component's selector that decides which picture shapes justify a download; (7) the downloader that retrieves envelopes over plain HTTP from the bucket's public endpoint, unwraps them and rebuilds data URIs; (8) the private editor-core helper that merges downloaded payloads into the editor's in-memory binary map (not the public wrapper that also invalidates shape caches). Then explain the flow end to end and answer: Is the size limit checked before or after the envelope is built, and on which byte count? How does a failure to load the storage SDK differ from one failed upload? What stops Bob from downloading too early, and which looser criteria apply on a fresh join? If a payload id already exists in Bob's editor, what happens, and why can a vector picture's revision change on arrival? Base your explanation on this checkout's implementation; do not modify code.
tasks.title: Picture bytes travelling between peers in a live room

tasks.prompt: Investigate this Excalidraw checkout. During a live session, Carol clicks Dave's avatar so that her canvas keeps mirroring whatever region Dave is looking at; whenever Dave scrolls or zooms, Carol's view moves with him, until she takes over the view herself or Dave leaves. Identify exactly 6 implementation functions by these semantic roles: (1) the editor-core method that announces a viewer's wish to start or stop shadowing a peer to the embedding host, through both an imperative subscription and a component prop; (2) the room component method in the hosted app that records the newly shadowed peer and tells the relay server to drop the previous subscription before taking out the new one; (3) on Dave's side, the room component method that conditionally publishes his current viewport rectangle; (4) the transport method that wraps that rectangle in an encrypted, fire-and-forget message addressed to a dedicated per-peer sub-channel rather than the room itself; (5) the element-package geometry helper that converts scroll offsets, canvas size and zoom into that rectangle in canvas coordinates; (6) on Carol's side, the shared editor-package viewport helper that computes the scroll position and zoom needed to frame a received rectangle. Then describe the full path from Carol's click to her view moving, and answer: Under what condition does Dave publish his rectangle even when his list of watchers might be empty, and what triggers that? What happens when Carol and Dave each shadow the other? Which framing mode does Carol's side request, and how does it differ from the default mode regarding zoom levels above 100%? Identify exactly 8 implementation functions by these semantic roles: (1) the editor helper, invoked at most once per drag, that clones the moving set, resets the originals to their press-time positions, swaps the press bookkeeping (hit target, hit list, drag origin) over to the copies, and replaces the scene synchronously; (2) the per-object cloning step that gives a copy a fresh identity and timestamps, optionally a new roughness seed, and remaps cluster ids through a shared old-to-new table; (3) the recursive structural cloner that handles plain objects and arrays but skips the top-level memoised drawing artefacts; (4) the tiny revision helper that increments the counter, rolls a new random tiebreaker and stamps the time without notifying anyone; (5) the reordering pass, run before cloning, that makes the members of every cluster contiguous level by level from the outermost cluster inward, keeping first-appearance order and bailing out if anything would be lost; (6) the post-cloning fixer in the attachment module that rewrites label, host and arrow-endpoint references to point at copies, drops references whose target was not cloned, and re-routes right-angle connectors; (7) the fixer that points each copy's artboard membership at the clone of its original's artboard, or at none; (8) the editor method that, only when snapping applies, recomputes the stored spacing between neighbouring shapes used for equal-distance guides. Trace the call path from the drag handler through these, then answer: After cloning, which set sits higher in stacking order, and which set continues to move? Right after cloning, which artboard does a copy of an artboard child belong to when the artboard itself was not cloned, and why? What happens to an arrow cloned without the shape it was attached to? Is the roughness seed randomised once or twice for these copies? Base your explanation on this checkout's implementation; do not modify code.

In normal mode it processes only elements not already pending and grows the pending set; in Alt/restore mode it processes only already-pending elements and shrinks the set. On a hit it uses the element's outermost group id to add or remove every member of that group, and it also adds/removes a shape's bound label or a label's host container. It first performs a cheap inflated-bounds overlap check using a threshold of 15 for freedraw and strokeWidth/2 otherwise, then treats interiors as hits when shouldTestInside(element) and the point is inside the element. Freedraw uses outline segments with tolerance Math.max(2.25, 5 / zoom) and falls back to polygonIncludesPointNonZero(pathSegment[0], outlinePolygon) for containment. Open polylines and arrows are tested segment-by-segment with tolerance Math.max(strokeWidth, (strokeWidth * 2) / zoom). Other shapes use intersectElementWithLineSegment against the shape and its bound text."},{"path":"packages/element/src/collision.ts","symbol":"shouldTestInside","line":87,"explanation":"Shared shape-kind rule for whether a shape's interior is touchable. Arrows always return false. It computes isDraggableFromInside as a non-transparent background plus hasBoundTextElement, an embedded/iframe-like element, or a text element. Lines and freedraw require that interior rule plus a closed loop; other shapes return isDraggableFromInside or isImageElement. Thus filled, labeled, embedded, and textual shapes have touchable interiors, closed loops do for pen strokes and lines, and arrows never do."},{"path":"packages/excalidraw/components/App.tsx","symbol":"getElementsAtPosition","line":6043,"explanation":"Point query returning every hit shape under a scene coordinate. It starts from non-deleted scene elements, filters out locked elements and text elements hosted by a container unless explicitly included, keeps those for which hitElement(x, y, el) succeeds, removes elements clipped away by an enclosing frame/artboard at that point, and finally moves iframe-like embedded content to the end of the returned array. It preserves the original z-order otherwise."},{"path":"packages/excalidraw/components/App.tsx","symbol":"eraseElements","line":10306,"explanation":"Release-time commit. It walks the pending ids and detaches arrow attachments: erasing a binding arrow removes it from the bound element's boundElements, while erasing a bindable element clears startBinding/endBinding on arrows attached to it. These patches use raw mutateElement because the code explicitly does not want separate history entries or multiplayer updates for attachment cleanup. It then marks pending elements deleted, also marking elements whose frameId is pending (artboard contents) and hosted labels whose containerId is pending. If anything changed, it calls store.scheduleCapture() once and replaces all scene elements, making the erasure a single undoable step."}],"flow":"Pointer down starts the eraser trail via eraserTrail.startPath. Each drag move is converted to scene coordinates in onPointerMoveFromPointerDownHandler and, because isEraserActive is true, is handed to handleEraser; that hook appends the point through EraserTrail.addPointToPath and passes event.altKey as the restore flag. The trail calls updateElementsToBeErased, which examines only the newest segment from the last two original points. Every candidate encounter is classified by eraserTest, whose interior behavior is governed by shouldTestInside. The returned ids become App.elementsPendingErasure and the canvas repaints, producing the fade. On pointer up, handleCanvasPointerUp records lastPointerUpEvent and the pointer-up handler calls eraserTrail.endPath; if the client-coordinate distance between pointer down and the final pointer up/move is exactly zero, it converts that point to scene coordinates, calls getElementsAtPosition, and adds every returned id to the pending set. Finally eraseElements performs the detached-attachment patch and the deletion commit.

The add/remove decision is made by the Alt flag plus set membership: without Alt, only elements not already pending are tested and hits are added; with Alt, only elements already pending are tested and hits are removed. This keeps the sweep idempotent and avoids repeatedly adding or removing the same element during one pass. The groupsToErase bookkeeping is needed because addition expands a hit to the whole outermost group. When giving shapes back, a hit group's entire membership must be removed and the group marker cleared; otherwise Alt-sweeping one member would leave the other group members faded even though the cluster was originally added as a unit. The marker also prevents re-expanding the same group on every move. Bound labels and label hosts are likewise removed together.

A zero-distance click removes every shape returned by getElementsAtPosition at that scene point, not merely the topmost one, subject to that query's exclusion of locked shapes and hosted labels, its artboard clipping, and its ordering of embedded content. Distance is measured as the Euclidean pointDistance (Math.hypot) between the client/screen coordinates of lastPointerDownEvent and the final lastPointerUpEvent or lastPointerMoveEvent, not in scene units. The subsequent eraseElements call also removes artboard contents and hosted labels for pending ids. Attachment detachment deliberately uses raw mutateElement instead of the normal history path so that cleanup does not create separate undo entries or multiplayer updates; only the final deletion is captured once via scheduleCapture, so the whole erasure is one undoable action."}

If just one selected element is frame-like (this checkout calls frames/artboards frame-like elements), it sets exportingFrame to that element and replaces exportedElements with getElementsOverlappingFrame(elements, frame, elementsMap); if multiple elements are selected it re-fetches them with includeElementsInFrames. It finally returns the frame plus a deep clone made with cloneJSON(exportedElements) branded as ExportedElements."},{"path":"packages/element/src/frame.ts","symbol":"getElementsOverlappingFrame","line":1013,"explanation":"The frame/artboard content filter. Thus shapes merely overlapping the artboard are included, while any shape explicitly owned by a different frame is excluded even if its bounds intersect the target; the target frame itself passes the test."},{"path":"packages/excalidraw/data/index.ts","symbol":"exportCanvas","line":99,"explanation":"Export dispatcher for editor settings. For png it encodes the canvas with canvasToBlob, optionally passes the blob through encodePngMetadata when appState.exportEmbedScene is set (embedding serializeAsJSON(elements, appState, files, 'local')), and calls fileSave; for clipboard it copies the PNG blob. Quota indicator: the out-of-space atom is raised only for recognized quota exceptions; on any subsequent successful localStorage write, saveDataStateToLocalStorage sees that it had been true and resets it to false, clearing the indicator. On a fresh load, initializeScene reads through importFromLocalStorage, loads files for current image elements, and calls clearObsoleteFiles. {"findings":[{"path":"packages/excalidraw/scene/export.ts","symbol":"exportToSvg","line":969,"explanation":"Builds the SVG vector document. It creates the root <svg> with version/xmlns/viewBox/width/height, creates the <metadata> and <defs> children, and prepends the svg-source:excalidraw comment. When config.embedScene is set, it calls encodeSvgBase64Payload with serializeAsJSON(elements, appState, data.files || {}, "local") inside try/catch, logging and swallowing any error so a failed embed does not abort the SVG. It then adds one clipPath (id = frame.id) per frame/artboard to <defs>, inlines font-face declarations into a <style> in <defs>, paints the background <rect> unless the background is transparent, and finally calls renderSceneToSvg on the prepared elements."},{"path":"packages/excalidraw/scene/export.ts","symbol":"encodeSvgBase64Payload","line":1194,"explanation":"Writes the embedded payload into the metadata node. It turns the supplied JSON payload into the compressed encoded record via encode({ text: payload }), JSON.stringifies that record, and converts it to base64 with stringToBase64(..., true). It then appends the marker comments payload-type:application/vnd.excalidraw+json, payload-version:2, payload-start, the base64 text node, and payload-end to the <metadata> element."},{"path":"packages/excalidraw/data/encode.ts","symbol":"encode","line":99,"explanation":"The text packer. It returns a versioned EncodedData record {version:"1", encoding:"bstring", compressed, encoded}. By default (compress !== false) it deflates the UTF-8 text with pako, converts the deflated bytes to a binary/byte string with toByteString, and sets compressed true. If deflate throws, it logs the error and silently falls back to an uncompressed toByteString(text) with compressed false, so encoding still succeeds."},{"path":"packages/excalidraw/data/json.ts","symbol":"filterOutDeletedFiles","line":34,"explanation":"Serializer-side asset pruner used by serializeAsJSON for local exports. It walks the elements and keeps a BinaryFiles entry only when the element is not deleted, has a truthy fileId, and files[fileId] exists. Thus a removed shape's referenced photo is omitted from the embedded files object, while photos still referenced by live picture shapes are preserved."},{"path":"packages/excalidraw/renderer/staticSvgScene.ts","symbol":"renderElementToSvg","line":97,"explanation":"Per-element SVG emitter. In the image case it computes a symbol id from fileData.id (image-<fileId>), or for a cropped image uses image-crop-<fileId>-<hash(uncroppedWidth x uncroppedHeight)>. It looks up an existing <symbol> by id, creates it only once with an <image href=fileData.dataURL>, and prepends it to <defs> (or root). Each occurrence is emitted as a <use href="#symbolId">; cropped images additionally get crop-adjusted use dimensions, a mask, and optional rounded clipPath. When renderConfig.reuseImages is false, the symbol id becomes image-<element.id>, so each occurrence gets its own symbol."},{"path":"packages/excalidraw/scene/export.ts","symbol":"decodeSvgBase64Payload","line":1221,"explanation":"Reader for embedded SVG scenes. It requires payload-type:application/vnd.excalidraw+json in the raw markup and extracts the payload-start/payload-end text; if the type is absent or those markers are missing it throws Error("INVALID"). It reads payload-version (default "1") and sets isByteString = version !== "1", base64-decodes the blob, JSON.parses it, and either accepts legacy unwrapped excalidraw JSON (no "encoded" field but type === EXCALIDRAW) or calls decode(encodedData) to inflate/decode it. Any failure in that inner path is rethrown as Error("FAILED")."}],"flow":"On save, the export action flows through data/index.ts exportCanvas, which calls exportScene({type:"svg"}) and sets embedScene from appState.exportEmbedScene for SVG. exportToSvg first assembles the SVG root/metadata/defs, then calls encodeSvgBase64Payload with serializeAsJSON(elements, appState, files, "local"). serializeAsJSON prunes the files object with filterOutDeletedFiles, so the removed shape's photo is not written; only assets referenced by live shapes remain. encode deflates the serialized JSON by default, producing the versioned byte-string record, and encodeSvgBase64Payload wraps that record in JSON and base64, placing marker comments plus the base64 text into <metadata>. exportCanvas then prepends SVG_DOCUMENT_PREAMBLE, saves the blob, and names it .excalidraw.svg when embedding is enabled. For rendering, renderSceneToSvg iterates shapes and renderElementToSvg emits image symbols/uses. On drop, parseFileContents reads the SVG text and calls decodeSvgBase64Payload; it locates the embedded block, distinguishes payload generations from the payload-version comment, decodes base64, JSON.parses it, and decode inflates it back to the original JSON text. loadSceneOrLibraryFromBlob then JSON.parses that returned string and restores elements/appState/files into the editor.

The embedded drawing is normally compressed: encode's compress parameter is omitted, so pako deflate runs, and the record has compressed=true. If deflation throws, encode falls back to an uncompressed bstring. The base64 conversion deliberately passes isByteString=true (for payload-version 2), because encode.encoded is already a binary/byte string whose characters represent raw bytes; running it through stringToBase64's default toByteString/TextEncoder path would UTF-8 re-encode those bytes and inflate or corrupt the data. A failure while embedding does not abort the save: exportToSvg catches encodeSvgBase64Payload errors, logs them, and continues rendering/saving an SVG without an embedded scene.

With the default reuseImages=true, the two picture shapes sharing one photo produce two <symbol> definitions, not one: the uncropped shape uses image-<fileId>, while the cropped shape uses image-crop-<fileId>-<hash of uncropped width x height>. The cropped symbol is distinct because it stores the full uncropped image at its uncropped dimensions and the occurrence is masked/clipped/dimension-adjusted for the crop. If symbol reuse is disabled (reuseImages=false), the id becomes image-<element.id>, so symbols are per occurrence instead of per asset; in this two-shape case there are still two symbols, but an additional occurrence of the same uncropped asset would create another symbol, and the image width/height are set explicitly to the uncropped dimensions.

The 'no embedded drawing' and 'corrupt drawing' outcomes are separated inside decodeSvgBase64Payload: missing payload-type or missing payload-start/payload-end markers yield Error("INVALID"), which parseFileContents maps to ImageSceneDataError("Image doesn't contain scene", code IMAGE_NOT_CONTAINS_SCENE_DATA). If the markers exist but base64/JSON decoding fails, the record lacks a valid legacy excalidraw type, or decode/inflate throws, it yields Error("FAILED"), mapped to ImageSceneDataError("Error: cannot restore image") with the default IMAGE_SCENE_DATA_ERROR code. For the oldest generation, payload-version is absent or "1", so isByteString is false and base64ToString uses byteStringToString, i.e. decodes the bytes with TextDecoder("utf-8") to recover the legacy JSON text before JSON.parse and the unwrapped legacy-data check."}

- To discover relevant file run `slopdex map -g "<glob>" -i -e "<term|term>" -q "<short symbol concept>" -q "<additional concept>" --private --callers 2 --callees 2 <paths...>` and immediately read plausible implementation ranges from the source files directly.
- Avoid mapping repeatedly, frontload the map in one call.
- Slopdex is not a replacement for other search tools, but an addition that provides semantic symbol search and mapping functionality.
- To rename or move symbols/functions or files, use `slopdex refactor <src> <dest>` with src an dest being a file and an optional symbol like `src/parser.ts::parse`. This correctly updates references for supported languages.
